verdicts.summary: The dead end the note describes is finding 0. The fallback link is set only after a successful Connect call, so a visitor whose Connect call fails gets only 'Use another account'.
evidence: apps/web/src/components/auth/ApproveAgentSurface.tsx:159-169 (link rendered only when environment is set)
apps/server/src/auth/McpOAuth.ts:410-422 (approvingSession returns undefined for a non-owner, so no csrfToken)

verdicts.summary: The redirect on the tunnel host is correct for the owner. Its only failure hazard is the non-owner dead end the note itself cites, which is finding 0. The redirect only fires after validateAuthorization succeeds, and it is gated by linked state, tunnel hostname and non-peer-link.
evidence: apps/server/src/auth/mcpOAuthHttp.ts:78-93 (hostedApprovalUrl gated on linked, not revoked, hostname match; errors fall back to none)
apps/server/src/auth/mcpOAuthHttp.ts:124-135 (validation first, peer-link exempt, own page as fallback)

verdicts.summary: Tried: a slow relay where the first authorizeDpopHttp (outside the 10s timeout), the request, the renewal retry and the second authorizeDpopHttp all run long. The loop, including the retry and its second authorization, sits inside one timeoutOrElse of 10s. The first authorization is bounded by getDpopToken's 30s timeout. Total bound is about 40s, and no unbounded network wait was found in the chain.
evidence: packages/client-runtime/src/authorization/service.ts:423-443 (token lock covers only local persistence, no network)

verdicts.summary: Tried: a hostile environment returns javascript:, data:, http to a remote host, or an https URL. javascript: and data: fail agentRedirectUrl, so followRedirect does not navigate and the page shows UNSAFE_REDIRECT. Server-emitted loopback URLs (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]) pass both checks, so no legitimate redirect is blocked. The client's LOOPBACK_HOSTS also accepts 0.0.0.0, which the server's rule does not, but the server never emits such a URL.
evidence: apps/web/src/components/auth/ConnectAgentSurface.tsx:50-54 (followRedirect navigates only when safe is non-null)
apps/server/src/auth/McpOAuth.ts:104-116 (parseRedirect: https or loopback, no userinfo)

verdicts.summary: Tried: Approve enabled before the timer fires, Approve stuck disabled after a focus event, and Enter-submit during the disarm window. canApprove requires armed, Enter-submit goes through the same gate, and the effect clears the timer on cleanup and on status change, so armed cannot stay false once ready. Deny is intentionally not gated.

The hazards are finding 7 (fallback to the code-only page with no code minted) and finding 6 (dropped Access-step messages). The open question has an answer: the wizard's remoteClients denial is effectively unreachable on the hosted path, because a hosted link requires Connect to be allowed, and Connect requires remote clients to be allowed. The server does not check remoteClients in the browser-session approval path, but that path is not reachable under the policy.
evidence: apps/web/src/components/mcp/UseInAnotherAppDialog.tsx:209-227 (remoteDenial and canMint messages dropped on hosted path)
apps/server/src/auth/McpOAuth.ts:410-422 (approvingSession enforces access:write only; no managed-policy check)
apps/server/src/auth/EnvironmentAuth.ts:1061-1066 (remoteClients refusal exists only for pairing-link creation)

verdicts.summary: Tried: a typed failure, a defect, and a thrown exception from the scheduler. Typed failures survive squashAtomCommandFailure, so isUnavailable works, and defects fall to the generic message. settleAtomCommandResult catches thrown errors, so run never rejects and connectTransport.send cannot leave the spinner stuck through an unhandled rejection.
evidence: apps/web/src/components/auth/ConnectAgentSurface.tsx:166 (load then-chain without catch, safe because send never rejects)

verdicts.summary: The peer-link exemption from the hosted redirect is not a server-side boundary. A peer-link client can be approved from the hosted page with a session decision, and the server never checks peerLink on that branch. The approval-code check only covers pairing-code decisions.
verdicts.scenario: 1) Attacker registers a client at the public /register endpoint with software_id equal to the peer-link software id. Registration succeeds if linked environments are on (McpOAuth.ts:343-349). 2) Attacker sends the owner app.t3.codes/approve-agent?environment=<owner env>&client_id=<peer client>&... (readEnvironmentId reads the URL param, ApproveAgentSurface.tsx:28-30). 3) The Connect approval call succeeds (no peer-link check in mcpOAuthHttp.ts:149-173). 4) The owner clicks Approve. approve() blocks only pairing-code decisions for peer links (McpOAuth.ts:452), so the browser-session branch (McpOAuth.ts:470-481) mints a code. 5) exchangeCode issues a session with peerLink true (McpOAuth.ts:541-546).
verdicts.consequence: A peer-link session for the attacker, after the owner clicks Approve on a consent screen that names the client. The consent screen does show the app name, and the own-page cookie path already allowed session approval before this change, so the new exposure is the cross-origin route to it.
evidence: apps/server/src/auth/McpOAuth.ts:343-349 (peer-link register gated only on linksEnabled)
apps/server/src/auth/McpOAuth.ts:447-481 (approve: peer-link check only for pairing-code)
